[[File:David Murray Gates.jpg|thumb|David Murray Gates]]
'''David M. Gates''' (May 27, 1921 – March 4, 2016) was an American [[ecologist]] who sounded early warnings that [[fossil fuel]]s, [[fertilizer]]s and [[pesticides]] posed a potentially fatal threat to the global environment.<ref name="MyUser_The_New_York_Times_March_12_2016c">{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/12/science/earth/david-m-gates-dies-at-94-sounded-early-alarm-on-environmental-perils.html?partner=IFTTT&_r=1 |title=David M. Gates Dies at 94; Sounded Early Alarm on Environmental Perils |newspaper=The New York Times |date= March 11, 2016 |author= |accessdate= March 12, 2016}}</ref><ref name="nyt-obit">{{cite web |title=David Gates obituary |url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/nytimes/obituary.aspx?n=david-gates&pid=177973101 |work=New York Times |accessdate=23 October 2019}}</ref><ref name="umich">{{cite web |title=Remembering former director Dr. David M. Gates (1921-2016) |url=https://lsa.umich.edu/umbs/news-events/all-news/archived-news/2016/03/remembering-former-director-dr--david-m--gates--1921-2016-.html |publisher=University of Michigan: Biological Station |accessdate=23 October 2019}}</ref> He published over fifty research papers and six books. His most influential book, "Energy Exchange in the Biosphere," is often called the Rosetta Stone for biologists studying plant-environment heat exchange.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Porter |first=Warren |date=July 2016 |title=David Murray Gates 1921–2016 |url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/bes2.1244 |journal=The Bulletin of the Ecological Society of America |language=en |volume=97 |issue=3 |pages=213–215 |doi=10.1002/bes2.1244 |issn=0012-9623|doi-access=free }}</ref>

He was the son of eminent botanist, Frank Caleb Gates and Margaret Murray Gates. David M. Gates began his career as an ecologist and academic at the University of Denver in 1947, where he was an associate professor working on radiation properties of the atmosphere and climate. This was key for his later work involving plant and animal interactions with their environment. While an academic, Gates also worked with General Motors as a “consulting ecologist” to discuss the company’s environmental impact.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=David M. Gates papers, 1910-2016 - University of Michigan Bentley Historical Library - University of Michigan Finding Aids |url=https://findingaids.lib.umich.edu/catalog/umich-bhl-0196 |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=findingaids.lib.umich.edu |language=en}}</ref> Additionally, he aided in the formation of the Clean Air Act of 1970. He was also one of the first people to speak out on greenhouse gasses warming the global climate.<ref name=":0" /> D

In 1964, Gates began to teach natural history at the University of Colorado. Here, Gates met mechanical engineer Dr. Frank Kreith. Together, they researched interactions on heat and mass transfer principles. Their work bridged biology and engineering, creating a new field known as biophysical ecology.<ref name=":1" /> Their later work together regarding "Radiation and Convection in Conifers" begged further questions involving plant-environment heat exchange, inspiring Gates to write one of his aforementioned most famous books, "Energy Exchange in the Biosphere."<ref name=":1" />

After teaching and researching at a variety of institutions, he landed at the University of Michigan as a professor of botany and to direct the University of Michigan Biological Station in 1971. Here, he exercised his excellent fundraising abilities to support the Biological Station. He also educated many future generations about environmental field research, ecosystems, and sustainability in natural systems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=David M. Gates papers, 1910-2016 - University of Michigan Bentley Historical Library - University of Michigan Finding Aids |url=https://findingaids.lib.umich.edu/catalog/umich-bhl-0196 |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=findingaids.lib.umich.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Gates was a physicist and ecologist, professor emeritus of biology, University of Michigan. He received his B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. degrees in physics from the [[University of Michigan]].
